name: Diaphragm
classification_notes: A high-contrast condensed serif designed exclusively for display use, rooted in Howland (John F. Cumming, 1892) but evolved into a contemporary form. The terminals fall between ball terminals and sharp serifs – an unusual intermediate. The Open and Stencil variants use progressive stroke erosion rather than a conventional stencil break.
summary: A condensed high-contrast display serif offered in Regular, Open and Stencil variants with progressive stroke erosion.
description: Diaphragm draws from Howland, an 1892 display typeface combining vertical and diagonal stress, though it has shifted considerably towards something more contemporary. The letterforms push hairline contrast to its limits and feature terminals that sit between ball and sharp serif forms. The Open and Stencil variants introduce progressive stroke erosion – gaps that widen incrementally between strokes – making the stencil concept structural rather than decorative.
foundry_blurb: Diaphragm began as a commission for Sabir, a literary journal whose narrow, elongated format called for a condensed typeface strong enough to carry a single word across the cover. Working from 1892 specimen sheets of Howland – an unusual display face combining vertical and diagonal stress – Antonin Bertrand gradually departed from that historical reference to produce something more rationalised and contemporary. Notable for its extremely thin hairlines and its non-standard terminals, the family expanded to include Diaphragm Open and Diaphragm Stencil, in which strokes are progressively eroded to open up gaps in the letterforms. Since its retail release in 2026, it has appeared on album covers, exhibition identities and other editorial work.
